utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can follow the proceedings in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Ann Sutherland, Joanna Korner, and Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. John Ackerman, David Cunningham, Aleksandar Vujic, and Cynthia Dresden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see you are not complaining of inequality today because you are four three and three on the other side. And good morning to you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I'll leave that alone, Judge. There is a matter I would like to raise though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner has advised me that she will not finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In view of that, let me -- I want to make this request. Could we stop at about 1.15 or 1.20 so that I can -- I'm still dealing with this dental problem that was rather obvious here one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem with us. I suppose it's not a problem with the Prosecution. I don't -- I don't even imagine it could be. I suppose it's not a problem for the witness either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The witness planned on being here over the weekend, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I planned on leaving on Sunday. I was told yesterday that the Prosecution would finish its case this morning. But I can -- I can certainly adjust to this new situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Professor Shoup. And that prompts me to say good morning --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to you. Welcome back. Ms. Korner will be proceeding with her cross-examination. And I suppose there's nothing else that -- that you need to say? You can proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can I just say, Your Honours, as -- I think there's a slight problem with the audiovisual unit this morning, which I think Your Honour heard. I am going to ask that a video be played very shortly -- part of a video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Four hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No. About 15 minutes. Oh, it is working. Well, my information is out of date. I'm told it's now working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's now working. Okay. I recognise Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is another problem, Your Honour, I neglected to mention. It's one of these goose/gander problems. We were given just a few moments ago, like ten minutes ago a list of exhibits that the Prosecution was going to use. You'll recall Ms. Korner wanting us to give her the list last Wednesday for the witness that was coming on Tuesday. And we don't get a list until this morning, so obviously we haven't had a change to pull these documents, look at them here -- I don't have them here. I can't bring thousands of documents to court. And it's a big problem. I don't think the court had the list either, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have a list except --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's absolutely right. It was an oversight on my part. Yesterday afternoon we intended to give Mr. Ackerman and the Court -- or yesterday evening -- the list, the potential list, I should say, because, of course, Professor Shoup said a lot of things yesterday which were not in his report and which obviously we want to check on. Your Honour, that's one of the reasons why, in any event, I said the cross-examination would have to go over till Monday, because over the night --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem for us. We are prepared to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very sorry about this. What we're going to do today is we've got copies of a lot of what's going to be put to the witness because they're, as it were, new documents. In addition to that, whatever is -- is an exhibit - and they're not that many on my list at the moment - we will put up on the ELMO from our side, and the witness can have the copies. But Your Honours will be able to see what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I do -- Mr. Ackerman is absolutely right. I think all I can say is it was a long day yesterday, and yesterday evening we just forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is a problem as we go along, Mr. Ackerman just point it out to me - and you know that we will try and find a way. So that shouldn't be a problem to anyone, and let's -- let's proceed. Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I just make a recommendation to you. I'm saying this from experience, because I don't want you to get carried away with the idea that Monday for sure this will be over. It very much depends on your answers and the way you will give your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to -- I usually give this advice to the majority of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to be as concise as possible. Please answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I see no reason why you should get excited about certain matters. I would imagine you are going to face quite a cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- so --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's how to put the witness off, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But it's just I am alerting the witness because I saw how he reacted to your last couple of questions. I mean, I want to make things clear, Professor Shoup, because we -- we are concerned about every person that -- that sits in this courtroom, including witnesses, of course, and sometimes primarily. So we are not trying to discerp people. We are not trying the Muslims in Bosnia or elsewhere. We are not trying the Croats. We are just trying an individual here. The historical part, of course, plays an important role, and that -- and this is why Ms. Korner's question was very pertinent last time, whether you have read -- whether you have been made aware of the contents of the indictment in this case, because basically we have, as the primary allegation, one of the main allegations by the Prosecution is that there was a joint criminal enterprise in which the accused was involved allegedly. So naturally the historical part assumes a very important -- an important role. But do keep in mind that whom we are -- who we are trying here, who is on trial here, is an individual and he -- he is being tried for particular specific crimes. So if you wish to get acquainted, to familiarise yourself with the contents of the indictment, I suppose we can give you a copy. I think it's only fair that at this point in time he should be made aware of what the indictment is all about. Because I -- I got the impression yesterday that he ran off the -- at a tangent immediately you put a particular question. And that worried -- you're experienced lawyers, both of you, and that -- and I am an experienced lawyer, we are experienced lawyers and Judges too. It put us on our guard immediately. And this is why I'm saying what I'm saying now. Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you in the meantime had a look at the indictment or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Would you like to see the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me explain my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was under the impression that the expert witness in this particular situation was to provide an historical background. I had a choice in preparing for this trial of either getting involved in the specifics of the indictment against Mr. Brdjanin - and I was not encouraged to do so - or preparing the report that you have seen in front of you, which deals with broader historical matters, and have tried to stick to that latter because I thought that was what you wanted me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are testifying, giving evidence in a particular trial, and you are bound to face questions which are related to the events that are the subject matter of this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. I just was under the impression. Nevertheless, I have seen expert witnesses testify in the case -- in the Tadic case. Professor Gow, for example, who did exactly what I thought I was supposed to do here, and that is to provide you with the -- and this is where my expertise lies. If -- the only place where we have -- might have overlapped would have been in a very detailed examination of Bosanska Krajina, this area, and you -- as you will see in my report, I did make an attempt to see in the scholarly literature what we know about this region during the war. I came up with virtually nothing. But I felt that if I focussed on -- on the indictment or particulars of the criminal actions -- alleged criminal actions that I really wouldn't be providing you with the expertise that I thought I had acquired over the years about the problems of Bosnia. It would be one or the other; I can't really give you both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will take whatever responsibility might accrue for Mr. Shoup not reading the indictment in this case. That was my decision. It's always been my position - and I think it's a correct one - that an expert witness has no business providing the Court his opinion of what the evidence shows, with regard to particular allegations in the indictment. That's the Court's job. And so I deliberately insulated him from the indictment in this case so that we could deal with matters that I believe were appropriate for -- for experts. I mean, if it's required that an expert before he can testify must first of all be familiar with the indictment and, second of all, know Mr. Brdjanin, then I think we can throw out all of the testimony of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're misreading me, Mr. Ackerman. That's not what I meant. What I meant is that within the macrocosm of the whole tragedy that occurred in Yugoslavia there is the microcosm of the events in which, according to the Prosecution, your client is involved. And those events basically, and especially since it's being alleged that a joint criminal enterprise came out, was hatched, because of these events, obviously form an integral part of this story. And the problem is -- the problem occurred to my mind in the first place, when I -- when I read through your client's report, your expert's report, and also through the book, and found very little that concerned the events proper that occurred between -- particularly between April and December of 1992. That did trouble me, because I expected that that was going to -- to surface at some point in time. So I don't know. I mean, I'm not suggesting or hinting that your expert should be made aware of the contents of the indictment so that he then gives us his expert opinion on those particular events and as far as they relate to your -- to your client. I mean, that's not the point. But it would make -- it would open a window for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it helps, I don't anticipate, certainly not today, as far as I can see, going into the nuts and bolts of the events with one or two small exceptions, which relate to various assertions made by the professor. So from that point of view, it's perhaps not necessary for him to look at the indictment. He may - it's up to him, of course - want to see it over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But let's do this. Madam Registrar, perhaps he could have a copy of the last revised indictment, and that would be made available to the witness, say, either in the first break, et cetera, and then he can have a look at it whenever he likes. I think he should be put in the picture, irrespective of whether there will be direct questions on -- on any of those events. But there are historical events that, of course, are not mentioned in his book, are not mentioned in his report, that are very pertinent to what eventually happened in Bosnia, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to be touching on some of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can imagine. I'm pretty sure you are going to be doing that. Yes, let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, and thank you very much, Your Honour. I was going to be explain the same thing to Professor Shoup about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That we have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, professor, I want to go back to the film that we spent all of Wednesday afternoon watching. You have pointed yourself during the course of the running of the film to a number of misstatements of fact of that are made during the course of this film; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that this film is a piece of propaganda dressed up to look like an objective overview of the events of that time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to say yes. However, a very valuable piece of propaganda because it reveals many real people saying real things about the conflict in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to come on to that, but I want to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is a third part to this film, is there not, which the Court was not shown but which you've seen because you've told us you've got the video?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You would -- I would need a little bit of assistance here, just to prod my memory about what that third part is. And then as soon as you tell me what it is, I can tell you more about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to show you a very short part of that third part, which was not shown to the Court, which deals with the filmmaker's view of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if the audiovisual unit is okay with it, I'm going to ask that it's played now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you pause for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that gentleman, sir, Professor, you were asked about by Mr. Ackerman last time.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to recall -- that is, is it not, a gentleman named Jatras?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You have to -- if the Court agrees, if the Defence agrees, I agree too, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think what I'm going to ask you to do, perhaps, if the Court agrees, is you say your video is at home and your wife's there and there's a name on the proper version of this video, to check that that is Mr. Jatras.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we can pause the video there. Thank you. We can stop it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the -- sorry, just going back to the transcript. Sir, do you agree that that film suggests, first of all, that the attack on Srebrenica was entirely the fault of Naser Oric's men?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree that the film suggests, in terms -- or by -- not in terms but by implication that no more than 200 people were killed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a little difficult, you know, for me to hear and to follow, but clearly they are trying to reduce the numbers of persons who were killed in the massacre, to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you are aware, aren't you, that there has been a full trial on this particular incident and indeed there is still a trial -- a second trial going on at this moment?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the trials that involve the leaders of -- the Serbs and that Srebrenica has come up. You phrased it as "a trial on Srebrenica." That confuses me a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the trial of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware in just general terms the trials of individuals at which this issue has -- has arisen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this: Have you ever read on the Internet any of the judgements that were handed down in any of the cases which have been decided since you wrote your book?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I have just completed an article on the origins of the war in -- the origins of the collapse of Yugoslavia. It took me six months to write. It was extremely difficult to do. I do have priorities. Issues such as this are not an issue for me. I just -- I despise this discussion of numbers. I think the -- the idea that you can reduce the number and somehow reduce the -- the crime, I don't -- I don't accept this at all. And I think we are in accord on that particular position. So that it -- to me the historical facts of the war are extremely important, but I have my -- I have my priorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I understand that. I'm sorry. You misunderstood why I asked you that. I'm not interested in the numbers about this, but the judgements recount the evidence which has been given to the Court by the witnesses who actually lived through these events, and they come to certain historical conclusions. Now, don't you think that's important for someone who's writing about the origins of the Bosnian war?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have followed these reports of witnesses in the press. I have -- I felt that I was reasonably well informed of what they were saying. If I was going to write an article on this, I would then turn to the judgements that were -- I'm not unaware of what the witnesses have been saying about the nature of the Srebrenica event, if that's what you're implying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Please, leave aside Srebrenica. That was just an example. There have been aware since the Tadic case a very considerable number of judgements in cases which have dealt with different areas of conflict within the Bosnian war. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the course of those judgements and appeals, the Court has come to certain conclusions based not only on the evidence of witnesses but also of documents. Now, didn't you think it was important to see what that evidence amounted to and what conclusions the Courts had come to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important if you are doing research on a specific case and wish to know exactly what happened. If you're not, you are as an individual informed -- to give you an example, I'm sure you're aware of the bulletins issued by the IWPR.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Institute for War and Peace Reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Professor Shoup, I think I better explain something.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause. Just pause, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think he should be permitted to answer the question. He was asked the question, he was trying to answer it. She didn't like the answer so she stopped him. But I think he should be permitted to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. That's -- that's unfair and Mr. Ackerman -- the reason I stopped him was because -- I'm just going to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Professor Shoup, it may irritate you, but you can't ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, I apologise. Yes. We agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, will you -- you wanted to give the answer.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is that in this mass of materials that -- about the Balkans, including historical materials, one has to pick and choose what one follows. What I have chosen to do in my case - and I certainly won't apologise for it - is to follow the bulletins that are released regularly by the IWPR, by the Institute for War and Peace Reporting, which has its own team right here. And then I look at these and I pick out things that I think are interesting and important for my own research and work. It would be impossible for me to spend my whole day trying electronically to track down testimony and even more difficult to find some of the basic documents which aren't available, as I understand, by electronic means.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll try one last time, Professor. I'm not talking about the actual testimony of witnesses. I am talking about the written judgements that are available on the Internet. I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's now said three times that he hasn't read them. I think we've worn that subject out, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know he hasn't read them. And I'm still trying to get an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why is that not important for your research?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because my research is focussed on particular problems at particular times. If I was doing an article on the Srebrenica case, I would certainly read all the documents that I could possibly get my hands on through the Internet. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you going to produce a revised copy of the book that you and Professor Burg wrote?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you no longer have an interest in the wider implications, that is, as a political scientist, the politics which led to the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how anyone could reach that conclusion from what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, all right.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, of course I have an interest. And I can document it -- excuse me. My position has always been that it's now time for younger scholars to fill in the blanks. And I can give you evidence, repeated evidence, of the efforts that I have made to try to encourage younger scholars to either uncover mistakes that we might have made or to fill in the things that we couldn't do. And you will notice, if you have looked at the book, at the back of the book I give my electronic address, pss7a and so on, with the hope that if there is something there that is wrong people will contact me through the e-mail. Unfortunately, very few people have done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in all fairness to the witness, Ms. Korner, following your question, I think he did tell us earlier on that he spent six months writing a paper or an article on the origins of the war and that's -- shows you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we're slightly sidetracking from the film, because I want to finish off on that. But did you receive a grant in 2000 for a project entitled "Bosnia and Herzegovina after Dayton"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you -- could you tell me from whom the grant was given and from where I was supposed to be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's from something called the National Endowment for the Humanities.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, did you -- I mean, whoever it was, did you receive a grant for a project called "Bosnia and Herzegovina after Dayton"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: You -- you will please be patient with me. I really have to look -- I've received grants during the course of the 1990s. I just will have to -- I'd be glad to answer the question, but you'll just give me a moment to -- so I don't get confused between the various places and the various things that I was doing. There are times -- but I don't want to say more than that at the moment. I'm sorry. I just have to check it out and see what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, are you writing either a book or a lengthy article entitled "Bosnia and Herzegovina after Dayton"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have written for the -- for these Stefano Bianchini edited volumes, as you have seen there, various articles relating to Bosnia, which touch on the question of Bosnia after Dayton. But I'm not writing a book -- I'm not writing a book on that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we go back, please, to this film. Where did you acquire your copy of the video from?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: My copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mm-hm, your copy.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't possibly tell you any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it from the Serbian Orthodox Church in the USA and Canada who advertised this film?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know that. I don't have any connection with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It was actually premiered, wasn't it, in about 2002?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, do you remember when you got your copy?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you to have a look at a review. Now, I accept straight away that this film got a very good review from somebody in the New York Times, Mr. Holden. I'd like you to have a look at another review, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like to have it handed out, please, copies of a document, a film review, "Yugoslavia, the Forgotten War." Yes, it's going to be handed out now. Your Honour, this comes off the Internet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to go through it with you. Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this review before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Tanzer is also a reviewer, is he not, for the New York Times? Do you know that or don't you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And it's headed "Film review, The Forgotten War review by Joshua Tanzer." And it starts off by saying: "They can't handle the truth. The horrid Serbian-American-made propaganda film 'Yugoslavia, the Avoidable War' wants you to think the Serbian-run genocide of the 1990s was merely a misunderstanding caused by poor public relations and bases its key conclusions on interviews with a collection of crackpots and racists." I don't believe it. Now, leaving aside the fact that clearly it also contains interviews with, as we've seen, Lord Carrington and Lord Owen. I want to look at some of the other people who appear on this film. We see the filmmaker. Do you see that by the side of the picture?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm confused. On page 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On page 1. By the side of the photograph. Yes, the still taken from the video.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The film was made by George Bogdanich, identified innocuously on the film's website as an independent documentary producer, reporter, freelance journalist and editor. But in addition, an Internet search shows that Bogdanich has spent years as a Serbian-American activist with groups --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, can you please slow down. Interpreters can't follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I'm doing what Mr. Ackerman did. It's very difficult when you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "With groups identified variously as Serb net and the Serbian American Media Centre. Bogdanich raised money for the film from the Serbian American community. There's nothing wrong with being a pro-Serbian activist, but you don't then release a three-hour propaganda film pretending it's objective and factual and fail to disclose your partisan background"? Would you agree with that, that you should disclose what your background is and how the film was funded?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree. I think it would be more important to be factual in the film, regardless of whether you disclosed your origins.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The film is built around interviews with a dozen or so talking heads. Some are respectable types, such as British diplomat Lord Carrington. The filmmakers play these up, but they're only a fraction of the total. A few appear to be left-wing NATO haters." And then it goes on, and this is the author's own view of these people. "Not one person gives a contrary view. What we're getting is essentially the Serbian Unity Congress reading list and speakers bureau. To mention five of the film's authorities, Nora Beloff, with 24 screen appearances and a dedication at the end, is the picture's patron saint." And then it describes her connection with the Serbs. "-- we saw briefly I think for one moment. Then David Binder, former Yugoslavia correspondent for the New York Times professes a lifelong affections for the Serbs and was like several others quoted in the film a well-received speaker of the 9th Serbian Unity Congress. He illustrated his lifelong affection in a letter to the New York Review of books referring to war crimes kingpin General Ratko Mladic as a superb professional." "Now, Mr. Jatras, apparently an Orthodox extremist himself, he once called Michael Dukakis a pagan for not following the Orthodox Church on abortion and attacked him for marrying a non-Christian, although he insisted he was not being anti-Semitic. This GOP senate aide is also the author of an anti-Muslim screed in the obscure "Chronicles" magazine and the Christian activist that calls Islam a gigantic Christian killing machine and says the religion grew from the darkness of heathen Arabic. He was also the key-note speaker at the Ninth Serbian Unity Congress." Now -- and it goes on to describe more about "Chronicles." You heard about this particular publication?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: What publication? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Chronicles."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian "Chronicles"?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's called "Chronicles."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know someone who describes himself as a historian and political scientist, Dr. Srdja Trifkovic?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Never heard of him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you didn't follow in any way the testimony that he gave in, for example, the Stakic case?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not followed, as I said earlier, testimony in these court cases. I have followed the reports on the court in the IWPR and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the -- it goes on to talk about Mr. Trifkovic, who was a spokesman for Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb government. But can we come down to the next part in heavy type. "The Americans, the Germans, the Croats, the Slovenes, the Bosnians, the Kosova, the Albanians, NATO, and so on and so forth, that's who's responsible for the Yugoslav tragedy, but never the Serbs. In three hours you won't hear a single source accuse the Serbs of anything disreputable." Do you agree that that is an accurate description, that last sentence?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I disagree. I'm not trying to defend the film as you know from my criticisms of the film. But there were moments when they talked about Milosevic's -- if I remember, but I may have it wrong in rather disparaging terms. I don't agree with your premise, and that is that they are trying to show things from a Serb position. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I agree with you. They're trying to show things from a Serbian point of view in the film.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, in that case, I don't think we'll bother to go through this, because it states the fairly obvious, what we can all see ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be made, however. Exhibit 2724.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm confused about the exhibit number. The transcript says 7434. I think Ms. Korner said 2724.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were right, Mr. Ackerman. That shouldn't be a problem, because it's only for the transcript This document will be 2734 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now -- one of the things --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, I'm really uncomfortable that the transcript still doesn't show that it's 2724. They've now made it 2734 -- there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 2724 now appears. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. And thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, one of the things that you said about this film, in fact, before I think it was shown. Yes, you were -- you were asked by Mr. Ackerman - this is page 16 of the transcript for the 4th of February. Professor, even though you've told us you disagree with some portions of the video, do you believe it can assist this Trial Chamber and in some cases amplify and explain your own testimony to be given later?" And you gave an answer explaining that the question of the Serbs was a very different and complex question which couldn't be reduced to a simple proposition, that Milosevic was waging an aggressive war for Greater Serbia. And you said, "The other thing is, is it shows you what the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia too were thinking. It shows you how they viewed this conflict. It's really very hard to get inside their minds and to see what they were thinking." Now, I take it, Professor, you are familiar with the six-hour documentary produced by the BBC called "The Death of Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I am not familiar -- I have not seen it maybe for a year or so. So that if you ask me about certain details, I wouldn't -- but the general -- yes, I've seen this on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you own that video?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's a very long video. It's -- I don't have a copy of it. The -- I use it -- I view it at the University of Virginia, where they have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why did you acquire the video of whatever that film was called?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Bogdanovic's film.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that it? Yeah. I think it's a very simple answer to that: The BBC film is available anywhere in most libraries. I am very interested in these little scraps that come through that appear and disappear. I save them as an archive. I have films from all points of view. This -- the BBC films are very easy to get.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you accept that the BBC, "The Death of Yugoslavia," was a balanced portrayal of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an excellent film.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, please, at just a short clip in the light of the answer that you gave to Mr. Ackerman yesterday -- Thursday. From the beginning of the -- part 3, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sound?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, stop it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have problems?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sound. It's always the same in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but sound is the most important part of this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yes, it is, or this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honours, this is a problem that has arisen before. Obviously Mr. Ackerman and Sanction are a happier mix than we are. But can -- Your Honour, could we rise while we sort this out? Because there's no point playing it without the sound. We need to get the technicians in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if it's a short while, we can stay here and wait. If it's not, we go out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know if anybody in the audiovisual booth can assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll rise for a few minutes. We are going to wait outside the courtroom. As soon as the problem is sorted out, please let us know and we will start again. --- Break taken at 9.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just mention again that after Your Honours rose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- we received an e-mail that what was being said in Court by everybody when the court proceedings should have been shut down was being broadcast. I don't know how many times we have had to raise this, but it -- I don't think it matters, but nonetheless ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I want to make sure, first of all. That was one of the reasons why I suggested to my colleagues to leave the courtroom in the first place, because I know that that could -- that could happen. The important thing is that this does not -- is not relayed to the public to start with. And please do pay the utmost attention to shut down immediately the sitting when the Court rises. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we've now managed to get the sound working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Ms. Korner, for drawing my attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have I gone deaf or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. We had the technician in here and the sound was actually working. We actually heard it, and now it isn't working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- Picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I propose to play of that film. And I'm sorry about the quality. For some unknown reason it ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Professor Shoup, having watched that, having reminded yourself of it, can you seriously say that the Serbs didn't have a chance to explain long before this film was made their point of view?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- the question startles me. We had negotiations conducted by the United -- European Community by Mr. Cutilheiro. We're all aware of that. There was ample opportunity for all sides to make their positions known.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I think you misunderstand. You told us on Thursday that the reason that we should -- that you thought the film "The Avoidable War" was a good one and one which the Court should watch was that it shows you what the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia were thinking, it shows you how they viewed this conflict.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doesn't that film show you how the Serbs were thinking and how they viewed this conflict from the mouths of the people themselves?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, perhaps I don't understand the question. The images of -- of the fascist Ustasha in World War II are very powerful. And these images were being transmitted to the Serbs in Croatia. And now we can see this on the film and how it looked. And I think we all agree that that would have an emotional effect on the people. I don't know that -- I implied much more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm getting confused.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Shoup, look, it may be that we all misunderstood your reasons for telling the Court they should watch "The Avoidable War." But what you already said was the other thing is -- talking about "The Avoidable War," is that it shows you what the Serbs in Croatia and in Bosnia too were thinking. It shows you how they viewed this conflict. It is really very hard to get inside their minds and to see what they were thinking.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We heard Karadzic, Seselj, (redacted), General Kukanjac explain exactly what they were thinking at the time of the outbreak, didn't we, in this short clip?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there is no contradiction here. They were themselves convinced they were fighting against the fascist threat from Croatia. They were also persons who were devious in their ways and extreme in their conclusions, but -- and in their strategies they would, just as everyone in this conflict, lie and so forth, but they -- they genuinely believed the things that you saw on that Serb propaganda film, precisely because it is the Serb point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Professor Shoup, we may be at cross-purposes here. You're not suggesting that when Karadzic told the BBC reporters, for example, in respect of the peace demonstration, that he told his men -- I've forgotten what the exact words were, to get ready, he was lying?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The context here is -- is confused. I'm not sure -- I'm not talking about him lying in that particular instance, but if he would -- he said -- I'll give you an example, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you -- because I mentioned it in the report. He said, "No, we're not engaged in ethnic cleansing. You know, we're just -- people are going voluntary out of this part of Serbia." That was just -- you know, that was a falsehood.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, you're -- you're referring to some specific incident that we just saw here where he's not telling the truth? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to try and get at this one more time.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What is it about "The Avoidable War" that you say discloses about the Serbs which was not available to anyone who watched the "Death of Yugoslavia" made some considerable years earlier?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: When one does research, when one wants to find the truth, you keep looking at everything. And I presume that there's something of that spirit here in this court. There will be emotional moments in this film, "The Avoidable War," which you might not see on BBC. You will get a chance to see an eminent professor such as Susan Woodward giving her opinion, not that the BBC wouldn't have her, but they didn't. It just so happened. You will see the pictures of Dubrovnik. It was not destroyed. I'm not sure the BBC shows that, you know, but you will see it in this film. The rule I have done -- I've followed throughout all my career in the research is look at everything to find what is important. You can disregard the rest. It's that simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think I'm leave this topic. Finally, Professor.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You agree this is a piece of Serbian propaganda. It is all the more pernicious, is it not, because it includes in it interviews with "respectable people" such as Lord Carrington and Lord Owen, and does not reveal the background of some of the other people who are speaking, such as Mr. Jatras?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I just don't -- I don't call that pernicious. I call that just another film. We've seen so many of these films. One always extracts what one needs of this. Now, if you are speaking of using this film for a broader audience, for example, showing it in a church or something like this, yes, then I certainly agree with you. From the point of view of the Court, the experts and so forth, this really doesn't amount to that much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll just leave that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move now to the report itself. And perhaps it would be appropriate to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's have a 25-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Professor, I'd like to turn now to your report.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first thing I would like to ask you, is when were you instructed to prepare this report? Just pause.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] One moment, Ms. Korner. Something has come up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I begin? Yes. Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of the sitting, please, we will reserve five -- five minutes to discuss dates when -- when you'll bring over your witness and when we will bring over the other two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to raise that, Your Honours, because we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead, Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you were about to tell us. When were you first instructed to prepare a report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last summer Mr. Ackerman contacted me. I must explain that at the time I was not in the United States. I was in Switzerland. It was not possible to do -- engage in any research until I returned to the United States in November.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And could you tell us, what were the terms of reference? Were they -- first of all, were they verbal or in writing?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: My goodness, I can't tell you. We were in communication with each other by e-mail, and we talked, I believe. I just have to refresh my memory. I'm sorry. I can't tell you. What proportion of each we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, in terms -- sorry, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You may misunderstand me. What were you asked to prepare a report on? What were your terms of reference?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not given any specific terms of reference, that is, prepare a report specifically on, let's say, Bosanska Krajina. I informed Mr. Ackerman that I -- I'd been in the Court before and seen how an expert witness gave his testimony - in this case, Professor Gow - and I think we assumed that I would follow then the -- what I had learned from that experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, I'm sorry, Professor Shoup, are you telling us that you had no instructions, either verbal or written, that explained to you what sort of report was required?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that I really don't remember. I think we had a general agreement on the issue that I would provide an historical framework, you know, for the events that were in question here. I wouldn't be -- I would be doing a disservice to the -- to Mr. Ackerman if I said no, I received no instructions. This was our general -- our general agreement. I would have to go through my e-mail to see whether it went further than that. We -- what I can say positively was there was no instruction that I should focus on Bosanska Krajina. The understanding was I should provide a broad historical framework.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you told us that "we had," that's you and Mr. Ackerman, "A general agreement on the issue that I would provide a historical framework for the events that were in question here." But you told us that you've never read the indictment, so how did you know what events were in question?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, well, we discussed that. I -- I know from the -- and the book indicates this -- I knew what had happened in general terms in Bosanska Krajina, at the start of the war, and we mentioned it in the book here, and we mentioned -- in fact, some of the really terrible, you know, events, they're right here in the book. So I was familiar with them -- I was familiar with them. I felt that I had to make a choice: Either to go into great detail about Bosanska Krajina. I was unprepared to do that. But I was prepared to provide a broad historical framework, and we -- and it was on the basis of the book. I think at one point we may have even agreed to that that the report would take off from the book and summarise crucial parts of the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It's right, isn't it, Professor Shoup, other than the broadest of outlines, you do not know anything about the events in the Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's unfair, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, if you'd tell us --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm expressing an opinion about your question. But those events are -- take place in the context of the issues which Professor Burg and I studied in great detail. We have reference here to testimony. We quote -- if -- you'll see that reference to Bosanska Krajina actually is based upon testimony here at the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Professor Shoup, just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm trying to take care of the interpreters' ears.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if you bang on the book and on the table, I don't think -- I don't think the interpreters will -- will -- yeah, will like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please try to avoid it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just briefly to make the point I just made: The references to Bosanska Krajina are actually taken from testimony in this Court, in the -- and which was made at the time that we were writing the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You refer briefly in passing to some of the things that were dealt with in the Tadic trial. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you -- I don't believe that our reference to the disappearance of the intelligentsia in the Prijedor area - I can't cite the exact page - was necessarily extracted -- well, maybe it was extracted from the Tadic trial. I just don't remember. That's all. But it was -- it was extracted from the -- from the testimony here in Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Shoup, you referred to the testimony of Hanna -- what was her name -- Greve in the Tadic trial.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go back, please. Do you accept that you didn't ask -- well, I don't know. Maybe I should ask you this: Did you ask Mr. Ackerman for any of the, if I can call it, the core documents that have been dealt with in evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I asked or he supplied them, I don't know, but I was given Professor Donia's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. The documents, the actual documents that came into existence at the time.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. No. No. I -- I would have avoided getting -- as I said repeatedly, I felt I had to choose, either to provide this broader historical analysis or to immerse myself in the details of the -- of the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well. Can I put it to you, Professor Shoup --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- for example, have you read any of the minutes of the assemblies that were held by the Bosnian Serbs, the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have only read testimony and cross-examination of Professor Donia relating to those minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But in connection with any of your researches, have you ever looked at the original minutes?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never had access to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, have you ever asked for access?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, in the context of our research, it was important to know that certain things happened, that there was ethnic cleansing. In our minds, Professor Burg's and mine, there was no contention about who did it. And if we had been worried about that, if we'd thought maybe there was a real problem there, maybe we would have done this, but it didn't seem necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I'm sorry, Professor Shoup, you've come here to give the Court the benefit of your expertise --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- on, if you like, the broader context of the events.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't you think it would have assisted you to have looked at the minutes of the Serb Assembly which relate to the -- the broader picture?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been delighted to read these documents. I am -- I am a researcher. I love to see original prime material. I don't think it would have assisted me in trying to write a clear coherent, insofar as it is clear and coherent, report concerning the broader issues related to the disintegration of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to come back to -- to this question in a moment. But can I just ask you this: Did Mr. Ackerman tell you that he had these documents?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I assumed he did, just looking at the testimony of Professor Donia, it was obvious there were these many documents that were being discussed. And indeed, reading Professor Donia's testimony in cross-examination, it was very difficult for me to understand some things because it was obvious that people were referring to documents that I had not read.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ask Mr. Ackerman if you could have a cite of those documents that were referred to by Professor -- Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said now repeatedly, I had to make a choice: Either to try to prepare a report about the disintegration of Bosnia in a limited time - that was only perhaps a month, six weeks - or to bury myself in the -- in this material related to the trial, the specifics of the responsibility of the defendant for doing this or that action and so on. It may be that we will now be able to write the kind of in-depth account of what happened in Bosanska Krajina, as did Professor Duijzings for Eastern Bosnia, utilising your documents. I would be delighted if someone would undertake that task. I did not have the time or the ability to do that, given what I thought I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But wouldn't it be possible that if you had a cite of these original documents that it might have affected some of the conclusions that you draw?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that, since I haven't seen that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know that. But as a respectable reputable historian or political scientist, Professor Shoup, don't you think that you ought to have looked hat these documents?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I should prepare a coherent clear report on what happened to Bosnia in this period. And I know from my own research experience or telling graduate students what to do, focus on the task. I would -- if I had months and months and research assistants and so forth, I would be delighted to have looked at these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor Shoup, I'm going to press --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hesitate to interrupt, but the Court does need to know that the Registry limited the amount of hours that Professor Shoup could -- could put into this project, so he had to limit what he could do, in terms of preparing his report. We were only given a limited number of hours. And that may not be true of Prosecution experts but that's true with Defence experts. So I told him his hours were limited, that he had to focus tightly, and that he couldn't write this definitive thing that Ms. Korner is suggesting he should have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, with respect, I'm not suggesting that the definitive --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But my point remain it is same, Professor Shoup. Given what Mr. Ackerman has now said, that you had only a limited number of hours, didn't you say or did it ever occur to you to say to Mr. Ackerman, "Look, I can tell from the documents that I've seen that Professor Donia was using that there are many documents which I have never seen which relate to the broader picture? I cannot, given those hours, prepare a proper report for you in that time"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate your question. I think -- I think it's appropriate, and I understand. I could say to you, "Yes, of course that's correct," but let me stress something that I stressed earlier in my testimony. My decision was to prepare a report based upon the book and then to see what new sources of information were available which might increase our understanding of the war in Bosnia. And this is where I spent my research time. If you know -- and I, in fact, have presented you people with documents that you never saw. You will acknowledge -- I'm sorry, I can't ask a question. The CIA reports. I make great efforts to find out -- and it was not easy -- to get the Dutch materials. It was all electronic. It is very difficult to do. With the assistance of the -- of the University of Virginia library, I was able to download these materials. And I thought that -- that something as -- as innovative and as really superb kind of reporting on Bosnia by Duijzings should be brought into my report. That's where my focus was. I apologise if I should have done it differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it brings me on to another point - although, I'm going slightly off the scheme that I had in mind - but the report and the book, do you agree are all secondary sources?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the implication that in some sense secondary sources are worse than primary sources. If you were an experienced researcher in this field, you know that it depends. Secondary sources may actually have brought together collated materials that you yourself, if you were searching for primary sources, could not possibly do. Let's take, for example, interviews with refugees or persons who have suffered from ethnic cleansing. There are thousands of such interviews. You have to rely on a secondary source that has brought this all together and understands it. You can easily get lost in primary sources if that's all you do. And you have to exercise your judgement on what is the most valuable document, is it a secondary source or a primary source.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting for one moment that secondary sources may not serve their purpose. But my question was simply: Do you accept that these are all secondary sources?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Certainly the vast majority of these materials, for instance, the Dutch study or the CIA analysis that I have used here are very valuable secondary sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you yourself, for obvious reasons, have not had the possibility to check the facts that are -- are contained in the report on Srebrenica by the Dutch or the facts that are contained in the CIA report.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, no. But then as it -- also as an experienced researcher, I know the people I'm dealing with. Professor Duijzings is a very reliable source. He's done a great deal of work on Kosovo. He's always been impartial in his studies. I have never seen anything -- reason to doubt what he has done. And I always consider it extremely important if someone has been in the area in question, as Professor Duijzings was. These are all the things that contribute to one's confidence in using the material. It might be that if I went to the original sources I would make a mistake. I wouldn't understand an order that was given -- a military command that the CIA immediately understands the significance of. I might not understand at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You had -- however, on this occasion, you had available to you original sources directly dealing with the topic that you were going to give evidence on. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you mean the -- I'm not sure what you mean. Let's take the case of the Donia testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm talking about -- pause, please, Professor Shoup. I'm talking about the documents that were referred to in the Donia testimony and which were available to you through Mr. Ackerman, all of those original sources were available, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But would they have helped me? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you chose not to see if they would help you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you my research strategy already. I don't think I have to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you can't remember what exact terms of reference were. How long did you spend on writing this report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'd say six weeks or -- no, I take it back. I began in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How many hours?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'd say at least 150. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you do all the work yourself or were you assisted?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did all the work myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, can I ask you, who is the "we" who is referred to throughout your report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an editorial we.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it means just that. I'm accustomed not to say "I" when I write my articles but to express myself in that -- in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that because it lends more weight to assertions that are made, if you say "we" rather than "I"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained, by the way, at the very beginning what the "we" meant, as you know, in the report. I said -- I explained, the "we" means Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because in the case of your book, there was a genuine "we." There was yourself and Professor Burg. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's precisely why I think on the first page of the report I explained that the "we" in question is Professor Shoup, in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that the references in your report are always, I think without exception - and you'll correct me if I'm wrong - to secondary sources in one form or another.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say the majority of them certainly are. I can't remember if -- where I might have cited something that could be considered as a -- as a primary source, but certainly you're correct. At least these are mostly secondary sources, and some of them, all the more valuable for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you -- in your opinion, Professor Shoup, is one of the criteria or something that makes an expert authoritative is objectivity?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. But I must -- if you're asking me a question that I must reply to fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I have said earlier, in this kind of research, where everybody is making claims and counterclaims, to sift through that material, you must read and look at everything. That documentary that we saw, which you said, and I agree, was Serbian propaganda, has some very valuable material in it. And so you look at that and you know that you need to remember that and include it in some broader framework which you need corroboration, of course, of what you're doing. So that I don't consider limiting myself to only primary documents or even only trusted secondary documents. I read everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But for the purposes of this report, you haven't read any primary documents.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know really. And I'd have to go through all the footnotes here. There are about 100 of them -- to answer that question. But certainly the vast majority of these sources are secondary sources, which are most relevant to the discussion in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the same really, doesn't it, by and large, applies to your book as well?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- I absolutely do not agree with that. The question is: What is a primary source? For example, our newspapers, which recount what is happening in Bosnia a primary source or a secondary source? I'm sorry. I'm not supposed to ask anyone questions. Certain newspapers were extremely difficult to -- to obtain during the war. Let me take the example of Oslobodenje. I went to extreme lengths with the cooperation of Mr. Zulfikarpasic, whom you know, to obtain copies of Oslobodenje published in Sarajevo because I thought it was an important, essential source. I wasn't going to argue or quibble about whether it was primary or secondary. I found it. I utilised it when I could. It so happened that the European edition of Oslobodenje, which very few people read, was much more useful and much more important. I don't know why I should quibble about whether that's a primary or secondary source.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you read Srpski Glas?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Srpski Glas?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no much --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of it. But for the moment it's not something that I've found immediately relevant in my research. It would take me a minute to try and think back now to when I might have encountered it or used it. I could probably find some notes, if there were some. But for the moment, and relevant to this inquiry, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, why wasn't the newspaper produced by the SDS and the Serbs relevant to your researches or anything you were going to write?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was relevant. And I felt that one of the gaps in the book, for example, was the -- to analyse the Serbian position, especially at the beginning of the war in the period we're talking about in Sarajevo itself. And when I was in Sarajevo visiting the institutes there, I asked them if they would provide me with -- with the news -- with the Serbian newspapers, you know, of that period, 1989 and 1990, and they agreed. But as -- as things worked out, we never were able to -- to complete that, that part of the research. And I think that's terribly important. I would agree this is one thing for us -- for a graduate student or someone to try to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Just -- Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Let's see what you have to say first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to point out, just for the record, what an insidious thing this is. We -- we have a -- we have an International Tribunal here which allows the Defence to have an expert witness but restricts the amount of time that expert witness may devote to preparing a report to a very limited number of hours, which then enables the Prosecutor to then accuse that witness of having done an inadequate job of research and having failed to look at an appropriate number of documents and having failed to do this and failed to do that. That's an extraordinarily unfair situation that's created by one part of this Tribunal, which then -- inadvertently, I'm sure, but does assist another part of this Tribunal to discredit that expert that they have so magnanimously allowed me to retain. It's just insidious and outrageous, and I wish the Court wouldn't permit it to happen, because it's totally unfair. If you want, order OLAD to give this man unlimited hours, send him back to Virginia, and he'll prepare the kind of report Ms. Korner thinks he should have prepared, but we didn't have the time to do that. We had to be very, very selective. And I think it's unfair now because of the Tribunal's restrictions to permit Ms. Korner then to beat up on this expert for not doing everything that she thinks he should have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question, apart from the inappropriateness of making a speech like this in the middle of cross-examination, my question goes not to just the report but to Professor Shoup's general researches for the book and altogether as being put forward as an expert on this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have -- we have taken note of what you said, both of you. Points taken. Perhaps the witness can explain also to us -- we're looking through the bibliography of works cited in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
