utterances.text: -- your book and the part -- I'm referring to page 469 "Newspaper, news services, and translations," relative to the question that Ms. Korner put to you, I note that not even for the purposes of the book in question did you ever make reference or consult the Srpski Glas. So it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's conspicuously absent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that fits in with my recollections. I might add also that we -- there are sources that we would consult or look at and then discard as not being relevant to our purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, so that it doesn't mean that we haven't looked at Srpski Glas, I can't remember, but it was not relevant to our research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just want to make sure I understand. Are you saying you may have looked at it and discarded it as not relevant or that you never looked at it or that you can't remember? There are three possibilities.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you what I -- I think is the case, Ms. Korner, and that is because in Sarajevo I made this effort to try to get the Serbian press - but I had to leave Sarajevo before we could do this - it seems to me that that was motivated by my awareness that I had not had an opportunity up until that time to see that press.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But since then -- or is there any reason why you didn't go to the offices of Glas in Banja Luka, if you were interested in the press?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is after the war, of course. And -- I -- you have to just understand a researcher has to have certain priorities, and half this book is devoted to the international community's reactions, the Cutilheiro Plans, the Vance-Owen Plans, an immense amount of research was going into that whole business of -- the interface between the International Community and the -- and the -- you know, the local environment. I mean, we have practically 1.500 footnotes in this book. That's -- and no one has really, I think, up till the time of the Dutch study, done a better job. So yes, there are limitations here. And I'm aware of them, especially the fact that we don't know the Serb position clearly on constitutional issues in this crucial period of 1989 and early 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've already told us that there should be objectivity by an expert. Can I ask you --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- a little bit about your methodology. Do you, first of all, define what the question is that you're asking? For example, as you've told us, have the Serbs been, as it were, vilified?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, one has to -- if you have experience, you have to work on intuition, as well as logic. Intuition told me that we weren't getting the full story in Bosnia. And that led me to search out anywhere I could information to see, for example, if there had been -- Serbs had been guilty of the same kind of treatment that the Muslim -- that they were accused of actually giving to the Muslims. It wasn't easy. And the one reason it wasn't easy was that Belgrade itself was not providing this information. And intuition told me that this was -- that we had to push and push in that direction. For example, to get the full story. We got a great deal of that story. The conclusions were not that the Serbs were better off -- didn't do anything. The conclusions were that, yes, under certain circumstances Serbs were victims. Now, we specified those circumstances. I can give you in great, boring detail how the detective work went through to find out these matters. And I'm pretty confident of the results.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Professor Shoup, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, you know, intuition counts as much as logic. If you're asking me how I pose a question before starting my research.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, that was the simple question that I asked you: Is it that you, first of all, pose a question - in this case presumably something along the lines of, have we been told the full story?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you then go on to define or identify the methods for answering that question?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given them to you. Read everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So therefore are you agreeing with me? You define the method for answering the question?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you how I pursue my research. I try to make sure that I read even -- even the propaganda can sometimes give you some very valuable insights. Sometimes I'm -- maybe I'm not being clear up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Professor Shoup, look, at the moment I'm merely identifying which you as a historian, a political scientist will understand, the methods by which you conduct your research which then leads you to present the material to the Tribunal or the world. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that. I will give you another example of the methods they use, if that's -- if that's what you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I -- Professor Shoup, believe me, I mean, you can give me the examples. I'm just asking for the straightforward methodology which you use and which is important, isn't it, for an expert?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then you'll have to let me answer, and that is intuition that some -- the full story isn't being told, contradictions in people's behaviour. One of the things that bothered us the most was Mr. Milosevic's switches on the Vance-Owen Plan, which did not appear at all logical. It took a lot of research to route -- to come to the final understanding of why Mr. Milosevic changed his mind so frequently. This was, if you will, just looking at the facts and saying, "Now, wait a minute, something doesn't make sense." This is what you do when you're an experienced researcher, and this paid off. I just don't know what more I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Professor Shoup, do you understand what I'm trying to establish? I think maybe I better start again.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm trying to establish what you as an expert historian, political scientist, what your actual method of approaching these matters is, not what you did, not in the specifics of this case. I'm on to that. But how you approach it. How you -- what your methods of research are. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. And I apologise if I'm obstructing this dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say, to clear the air: First and foremost, having been subjected to -- for years to the -- all this debate about the national question in Yugoslavia, it was objectivity, to be -- to stand aside and look at the situation and not get involved on one side or the other. And this is what Professor Burg and I agreed to do. He actually -- he and I come from different backgrounds. It seems to me it was quite an accomplishment for the two of us to sit down and to be able to agree on the objective facts of the case. But it was absolutely, always let's see, let's not take sides, let's see what we can take by taking that impartial position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to try one more time, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that yes, you did have a question, and the answer -- or the question was: Have we fully been told of the facts? I've lost your exact answer now.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you then define or identify what methods you would use for answering that question?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I can only say in the chaos of this war you could turn to the press, you might look at television. But I just always felt that -- you could -- you could always have -- extract some useful information from even the most trashy sources. And I just don't want to repeat that obvious point. But we seem to be talking past each other. I apologise. I just don't understand any further what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before you went into this, did you sit down and say, "Now, how can I best answer this question?"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would depend on the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. The question you yourself posed apparently: Have we been told the whole truth?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you before you went anywhere sit down and say, "Now, how best can we answer this question? What are the sources of information we should be looking at?"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to give the example --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, did you ask yourself that question? Not what you did.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. You have to, depending on the question that's being posed. You know, the -- are we dealing with the International Community? Are we dealing with ethnic cleansing? Are we dealing with the events of the war? Each question means that you have to look at -- somewhere else for the documents, and maybe UN documents in one case, maybe newspapers in another, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. So the next -- would you accept that the next stage is to collect the sources of information which are relevant to the question that you are asking?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree you should then study those sources of information, applying to them the appropriate analytical techniques?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would be hard put to disagree. Mm-hm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And only then reach conclusions based on the application of accepted scholarly methods to your sources of information?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand -- I do understand what you're saying. You have to adhere to rigorous standards and to try to reach the truth. But I must insist that scholarly research depends also on intuition and experience. Something doesn't look right and so you pursue this matter because it doesn't look right and you want to find out what the truth is. It's not just simply simple logic to do research. It's also, as I said, experience, intuition, doggedness, you name it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that a number of -- of the conclusions you reached were through sitting down in people's kitchens and talking to people.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not about -- not in this book or in the report. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, in the evidence that you have been giving the Court -- and this is what you told us yesterday. Do you think that's an appropriate scholarly method of obtaining information?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- I never used it for any -- any report or book or article. I -- I made that comment in the context of peoples remembering events of the past in Yugoslavia or in the context of the -- of the point that people have set views on the national question, which it's very difficult to change. This is an observation that I can validly make on the basis of years and years spent in Yugoslavia. It certainly is a correct one. But it's not here in the book; it's not in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn to the beginning of your report. Do you accept that it is important that when making assertions of fact in a report, a book, an article, that should be accurate?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's terribly important, and it's terribly difficult not to make mistakes in doing research on a confused situation like the Bosnian war, which is, I repeat, why I included my e-mail address at the back of the book and said, "Anyone who has something to say about this" - and I was -- I was very acutely aware that we could have mistaken something inadvertently -- that they should let us know. And we didn't get much contact, but I am very aware that there will be, in the nature of the beast, things that -- well, can I give you an example, of something that went wrong? Is that appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want -- I want to deal now with your report, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you -- this is how many years on, five years on or more of your -- since your book was written.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In your report, were you careful to be accurate about statements that you made in that report, which are not statements of opinion but statements of fact?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly tried. I may not have fully succeeded, but I can assure you that my intent was honourable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's of course important, is it, to be accurate in your citations and your quotes?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is. We have already discovered that one statement I was made - it was brought up yesterday or so - really should be reconsidered about the persons engaging in acts of retribution simply because of what they heard before. And I'm -- I'm perfectly willing to accept any other criticisms that you might have of the report in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to -- you brought that up yesterday. Is it -- I don't know, we got this report about a week or ten days ago. That's when you finished writing it.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why in -- what suddenly changed your mind in the ten days?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: About that sentence you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, well, one thing was to go over carefully what Professor Duijzings had been writing. Remember, again the Dutch material is just fort of coming in now. So far as I know, many people in here in this courtroom have not read it or seen it. And so I was assimilating that material. And then as I read it, I realised that Professor Duijzings, for whom I have tremendous respect and who probably knows more than anyone about these problems, is warning us not to assume certain things. And I felt that I had gone too far at that point. And this -- this happens all the time, of course. And -- and hopefully in this discussion this morning I will find out other things. I'd be very grateful and appreciative if you will find out what's wrong with the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I'm sorry, Professor, what I'm asking you is: This -- it's not as though this report was written months ago. And you had -- you've referred to Professor Duijzings all the way through.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why did you suddenly change your evidence -- or, I'm sorry, your view on a sentence you can't have written more than a matter of weeks ago, if that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the -- the purpose of the report was to start with the book and then to open up controversial issues, Ms. Korner. And these -- such things as: Was it a civil war? Who was responsible? Is there such a thing as ancient hatreds playing a very vital role. And the reason these subjects were there is because they are controversial. Because I'm not going to claim that I have the last word on this. I always approach something like this as I would giving a paper at a seminar: Now let's discuss it. Let's see what's right and what's wrong in it. It is based upon my knowledge which is not small about what happened there, and I think it should be treated with respect and so on. But it's also, as we know from scholarly efforts, never completely flawless.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, I'm sorry, Professor, do you understand the difference between giving a seminar to a set of students and giving evidence in a trial of a man charged with the most serious of offences?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. And I'm not in this report dealing with -- with Mr. Brdjanin. And it's precisely why I didn't want to get involved in the documents, because -- of Bosanska Krajina and the activities of the defendant. Because I respect his rights and I don't want to make any false statements. I am doing something else here. I am hoping that we can open up our minds to the complex events of Bosnia, that they weren't simple, and in this fashion I'm entering into areas which are controversial. I don't deny it. I might even myself have -- have on occasion said something about this that I would like to discuss with the Court and have them listen to my opinions and -- and discuss them. These are -- these are very interesting, very difficult subjects that I chose to treat, simply because I think the Court is interested in them. I would never equate this with making a statement about the defendant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Can -- can I ask you this, Professor Shoup: Is the reason that you agreed to give evidence, given the restrictions or prepare a report given the restrictions that Mr. Ackerman so graphically outlined was so that you could have a public forum for putting these controversial propositions forward?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Of course not. I've -- I feel that the practice of having an expert witness for the Defence is an excellent practice. Presumably it provides a context in which we can divorce ourselves from the propaganda and so forth that we see all the time. In my case, one of the primary reasons for -- for writing this was once more to remind the Court that there was a great deal of negativism about the Serbs to the point that sometimes even a good Serb couldn't get an audience. Yes, I agree that that was a sort of political motive in all of this. But my own research has always been dedicated to absolutely showing both sides of the question. I think this is what my testimony indicates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were you shown, before you told us what you did consult to write this report -- were you shown either the report or the testimony given by Dr. Patrick Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you've read that as well.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, it's difficult, I must say, to understand a great deal of the testimony, because they refer to documents and events that you may not be familiar with, but I did my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who may not -- you mean you're not familiar with?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But these are -- these are, you know, the minutia of meetings and relationships between various bodies in Bosanska Krajina which an outsider outside of this Court wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Professor Shoup, but the report prepared by Mr. Treanor, which you say you saw, is nothing -- it has to do partly with the minutiae, as you put it, of meetings, but it deals with the whole question of the Bosnian Serb leadership, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take a step back. There may be a misunderstanding. I did not read his report. I read the -- the testimony on the report. And this -- if you -- so I would love to see the report. I would love to see Mr. Brown's report. I think those are both very interesting documents. In the event, it was not possible to do so

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I need to -- to have this clear. Let's start with Professor Donia. Did you -- what were you given by Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was given testimony by Professor Donia. A great deal of that was cross-examination. I've not discussed this in my -- very much with Mr. Ackerman, but there may even have been -- he can tell me -- he can tell you better what he sent me, whether it was everything that Donia said or not. I just -- there was a good deal of the cross-examination. There was some testimony by Dr -- by Professor Donia. Was it all of it? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you also receive the report, his written report. Professor Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would just have to -- I -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I want to make clear, Professor Shoup, is this: Because when you were asked about Mr. Treanor's report, I got the impression - I may be wrong - but I got the impression that you went through his testimony here, not report. But did you have the report available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. So in the case of Professor Donia, you went through his testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, pages and pages of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you have his report available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do apologise to the Court. These pages and pages of testimony were in front of me, and I just -- I know some of the things he said, but I can't tell you exactly, was it from the report, was it from the cross-examination and so forth. I would have to look at the documents to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Brown, Ewan Brown, did you go through his testimony?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I saw his testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But not his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not his report. Okay. I think that's pretty much clear. Ms. Korner, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you think it's at all possible, Professor Shoup, that if you'd asked for and read the full report of Dr. Treanor on the Bosnian Serb leadership, the full report of Dr. Donia, as opposed to the testimony, which was only partially dealing with the report --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- you might just possibly have changed your mind over the fact, as you assert, that the Serbs were the subject of demonisation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I would have change my mind at all. The reasons for that lay mostly by the treatment of the Serbs by the Western media. And to give you an example, I've noticed in the CIA report that they still state that the Serbs committed the Markale massacre. When I say that I can't believe it. There is no proof of that whatsoever. Those were the things that I've had to fight against for years. I don't think the Brown report would have changed any that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Mr. Brown's report. I'm talking about Dr. Treanor's report and Dr. Donia's reports, only which were partially brought out in examination and cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't you think -- just listen, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That you might have changed your mind if you'd read that report and looked at the documents, that the allegations that Serbs committed - I'm putting it at its lowest - crimes was a true one?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never said that the Serbs didn't commit crimes. That was never an issue. I -- it was not necessary for me to read the Brown or the Treanor report to find out the Serbs committed crimes. You will see it right here in the book that we document this and are fully convinced that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So by the phrase, on page 2 of your report, that one of the authors, namely, yourself --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- feels that the Serbs were the subject of demonisation --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- what do you actually mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that a Serb who has valid reasons to believe this or that or to give testimony in this court faces a tremendous obstacle. He's -- he's going to -- there is going to be, in my mind - I could be wrong; please correct me if I'm wrong - there is going to be a hidden bias against him. Now, when it comes to demonisation of the Serbs, I lived through this period when the Christian Science Monitor was ascribing the destruction of the bridge at Mostar, of all things, to the Serbs. I have seen this evidence in this Markale massacre, one of the, you know, really goriest events which upset everybody worldwide being treated as though, well, so we think the Serbs did it, so we'll just it at that. I find that accept. I mean. You can choose your words, "demonisation" or something else. It has bothered me. I don't have to excuse myself of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you read the judgement in the trial of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would love to. I've considered that extremely important and I wanted to. I've discussed this with Mr. Ackerman because of the difficulty in electronically downloading this material. And he told me that I could download this and condense it in Acrobat, put it on the hard drive and then read it. We went through a lengthy discussion on this. So that I hope I would be able to handle this electronically in the future. It's intimidating, as you perfectly well know yourself, downloading pages and pages of documents, and -- and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You go on to say, at page 2 in this paragraph: "Feels that the Serbs were the subject of demonisation and doubts that genocide is the appropriate term for atrocities committed by the Serbs during the conflict."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, leaving aside that "genocide" is a legal term, as you appreciate, Professor Shoup, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not a legal expert but I'm free to express my opinions about this. And that is simply that looking at the history of what happened in the Balkans and seeing what happened in World War II when whole villages, including women and children, were obliterated, this is my definition of "genocide." If and where that happened in Bosnia during this conflict, I will readily agree with anyone who says that this has the -- all of the characteristics of genocide. If we're talking about ethnic cleansing, and automatically associating that with genocide, I feel this is a crime against humanity and not -- don't see any reason why I should be ashamed to say that -- rather than genocide. But there is a further point I must make. And I'll slow down for the translator. Because I have been for so long associated with this field, I know how many times the -- the accusation of genocide has been utilised as a purely propaganda weapon. It was used by Milosevic against the -- what was -- against the Albanians in Kosovo, saying that the Serbs in Kosovo are guilty of genocide. I have seen it used in the western press recklessly, by people who don't understand that rather than being a -- a concept in the Balkans, which has this noble past in the Holocaust, it is actually a concept that has been degenerated and been abused over and over again. I'm -- and for this reason, I must be careful in using this term. I see it from the perspective of those people who have misused that term so frequently. That's -- I have no apologies, therefore, for being reluctant to accuse anyone of genocide.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, can you make a longer pause between the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation Continues] ... You don't know, do you, the exact nature of -- I put it -- most of the events that took place, for example, in the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our book --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, leave aside your book, please, and just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because that's where we deal with this problem. I have to refer to it. In our book, it is clear that persons were liquidated, intelligentsia, professors and so forth - at least, that was our conclusion; if I'm wrong, I apologise, to the Serb side in this case, but that was our conclusion - that struck a chord. That reminded me exactly of what happened during World War II. And it -- there are subsequent articles which show you, in terms of the numbers of missing people, for example, who have never been found - which is a very serious indication that something terrible happened to them - they'd even put this on maps. You could see that Prijedor is one, as you would agree, one place where that is evident; Eastern Bosnia is another. And these are -- these are -- this information I think is indisputable. I'm not sure what would be gained by asking me to go -- to go any further, since we all agree on what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking you now: Do you know, for example, what happened at Mount Vlasic at the beginning of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been -- I'm becoming a little bit more aware. The Kozarac events, remember, were -- were covered in great detail during the war itself. Mount Vlasic less so. I'm becoming more aware of that particular incident by -- by just what I see here in the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened at the Grabovica school in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened at the Velagici school in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Professor, I just want to look at a few things in your report.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I will, in fact, finish today.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 7 of your report.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the top paragraph, you say: "In March --" it's the third line down.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In March of 1992, Vladimir Srebrov --" would you go to the footnote, please. The pen name. His real name was...

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't ask the right person. I think it was Pavle Nikolic or something. I'm wasn't sure. Someone here in the Court must know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Milan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Nikolic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you didn't check that footnote?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, it would have taken a long time and there were more important things to do, and I thought the Court would understand it. In this case, it was not as crucial as some other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In addressing a meeting of Serb intellectuals penned that memorable phrase," and you quote it --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Iza jas provejava smrt."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to have a look, please, at the original article and a translation.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a new document. Your Honour, may that become Exhibit P2725. Your Honour, I didn't exhibit that third part of the video, but I don't think -- unless anybody wants it to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it needs to be extracted and made an exhibit because it's part of the evidence in the case now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm quite happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would think -- I would tend to agree with Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then it's P2727 -- 2726, the video of the third part of the film, whatever it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume that copies of the CD, the extracted CD, will be made available to all of us?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it must be on CD. Were you running a video or CD?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Running a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But we can probably put it on CD for you. But you've got the full version anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do have the full version. I can find it. It's no problem. Anyway ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree that's the article you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's very moving.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment. What does it actually say at the top? Does it read as follows: "The speech that Vladimir Srebrov wrote for the Congress of Serbian Intellectuals in Sarajevo but did not deliver," because he was not invited?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was not there in person, and that's why I say here that he wrote this. But I didn't say he spoke --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If you look in your --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I indicate that he was there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Just a moment. Look at page 7, first paragraph: " Vladimir, in addressing a meeting of Serbian --"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's a mistake. I was aware that he wasn't there. When I say "penned the memorable phrase" that was meant to say that he wrote it. No, he was not actually there. That's not correct. I knew that. He was not there. He -- he gave them this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Professor, you may at the end of all this want to go back through that report and correct errors that we may not have seen ourselves, but anyhow --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd be delighted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If this is changing the nature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the important thing is that - as you agree, that this is what he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. "What Vladimir Srebrov wanted to say at the Congress of Serbian Intellectuals and was not allowed to say."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we just look at some of things that he said in this.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look at page 2 of the translation, that is --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Intellectuals are not present at this gathering. They were never sent the invitations for this gathering, nor can they be found in the SDS Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, organisers of the current congress. They are the -- in the extra-parliamentary Serbian opposition. They do not want to take part in the slaughter of the Serbs into which they are being pushed against the local Muslims and Croats by the Mafia gang headed by Karadzic, Krajisnik, Ostojic."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: So on and so forth. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you look, please, at page 3.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not numbered -- oh, yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the bottom.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: About halfway down the paragraph, a very long paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In spite of all the threats and harassment that the Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina were subjected to during the several days prior to the elections of which they informed me either in person or on the phone, mostly from two regions, Bosnia and Bosnian Krajina, less from Herzegovina, they're crying, pleading their fear of repression by the SDS BH activists forced me to publicly demand the following: Leave the Serbs from the BH alone. All of you who want a Greater Serbia in this area who want some kind of a Serbian state of BH, leave here. You have no business here. Even more so, since you are making fools out of the uneducated Serbian population, creating genocide, turning them into ethnocidal people, turning them against their neighbours and relatives." Now, this gentleman, Mr. Srebrov, or whatever his name was, was a Serb, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And his view, expressed even in April of 1992, was that the SDS was effectively turning ordinary Serbs into people who were willing to kill non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is his view, I guess. I -- the reason that -- that I am glad to see this testimony is because I speak in the report about persons who went over the edge, exclusive nationalists, as I call them. And I don't excuse any of these people. And apart from the specific accusations that Srebrov was making at this time, this was a path to disaster what these people were projecting for Serbia. The idea that they're committing genocide I think is -- is -- as Srebrov says here, is to me not quite correct, but I understand his emotion at this particular time and I associate myself with it completely. I wouldn't take this document as a -- as proof of any one particular fact in any one particular place. Like everything else, I would compare it to what else I've known and see. The reason it's here is not because of the facts in the document but to show you how or where people were that they were headed for disaster. And Srebrov in my mind was a hero. I wouldn't have otherwise, you know, sort of, for no reason at all provided this sentence for the Court to -- to examine. I really admire him tremendously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. Can we go, please, to page 8 of your report, where you quote from your book.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Yes, okay. This now is the -- the "we," meaning Professor Burg and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you quote there part of the section "Introduction, ethnic conflict and the moral question in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You didn't go on to quote what you say on page 12, did you? Would you look at page 12 of your book.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. I'd be delighted to do that -- certainly whatever it is. I'd be delighted to read it to the Court, if you want me to. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The paragraph beginning: "Of the three nationalist forces, however, the Serbs have come in for special opprobrium."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Where is that? Which paragraph? One, two --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph on page 12, chapter 1.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I'm just not finding this sentence that -- where you're starting. I'm familiar with the paragraph, of course. Oh, I see. Yes, at the beginning of the paragraph. Excuse me. Yes, I'm now with you. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The focus on Serb behaviour that dominates most of Western discussion of the war is not, as some believe, the result only of better propaganda by the Muslims. It arises out of the fact that the Bosnian Serbs engaged in ethnic cleansing on a greater scale than the rest."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Although, as our account will show, Serbs in Bosnia were also the victims of ethnic cleansing." That's what you said then, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you adhere to that now?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That was the conclusion we reached, and nobody has changed our minds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that -- you go on to say further on that "The Serb nationalist leaders, along with the Croat extremists, were bent on destroying the multi-ethnic society which in the last analysis was the greatest accomplishment of Bosnian history."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That, I -- I don't -- I have doubts that I would put it this way any more. You may have noticed in my testimony that I've come to the conclusion since then, knowing more about what happened after the elections and the -- the struggle for power in the localities, that, as I have said to the Court, probably multi-ethnic Bosnia was destroyed even before the war began. That's what I say here, and that's something that's developed in my own thinking since the book was written.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you move, please, to page 14. Again, it's a question of footnotes that I want to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You are discussing -- well, at page 14, the report of -- I'm sorry, it's slightly before that. But we can deal with that. The report of the expert witness for the Prosecution. Well, you hadn't actually read the report, we now discover; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't be sure. I had a mass of paper, and I don't know whether, you know, I was reading the report at one and then going into the testimony. I'd have to go back and just see. I just don't remember. I'm sorry. I -- I just don't want to guess, Ms. Korner. You can appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, you know Dr. Donia very well?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say -- you were talking about -- it's the sentence before: "The Croatian national cause was quickly embraced by the Western Herzegovinians who had broken all ties with central government in the fall -- as early as the spring of 1991 and formed a Croat Crisis Staff in the fall of that year while at the same time organising paramilitary units to defend the region."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page are we on? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of your report.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And footnote 34 states: "On the formation of the Crisis Staff, See CIA "Balkan Battlegrounds, Volume I," page 133. Now, I'd like you -- to show you Volume I, 133, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you tell us where we see -- and I'm asking this genuinely out of curiosity.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Sure, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where do we see anything on that page about Croatian Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see. Here -- they deal with the Croatian -- Bosnian Croat -- it will take me a minute, if you don't mind. Let's see what's going on here. I think, without delaying the Court here, I think what's happening is that the reference is to the -- to the part of the sentence that deals with paramilitary units and not with the Crisis Staff. It may appear from the -- from the footnote that it -- that it's dealing with both of those facts, but it -- it's not. As far as I -- it's dealing clearly with the military side of ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So -- I'm sorry, but you appreciate, Professor Shoup, that this is important, because clearly one wishes to check references and check cites. It's important that we know where you're getting the information. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. There should have been another footnote in just -- two footnotes, instead of one, about the -- the footnote for the formation of the Crisis Croatian Staff should have been footnoted, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I'm sorry, I missed out one part that I meant to ask you about. Could you go back to page 6 of your report, please, and the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just move -- mark this footnote. Mm-hm. Yeah. Excuse me. I'll get there. I'm a little slow. Yes. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that second paragraph, you say this: "The -- you say: "The rational course of action -- this is paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would have been surely to put aside differences over the future of the Bosnian state and focus on saving Bosnia and avoiding civil war.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, leaving out the next sentence: "To whom was one to turn?"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The army JNA that remained in Sarajevo at least on the sidelines until April of 1992."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, Professor Shoup, that's inaccurate, isn't it, because the JNA, or as you called it, the Serbian army, had been engaged in the actions in Croatia against the Croats?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I -- I don't understand what that has to do with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, you say "That remained in Sarajevo on the sidelines."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may be --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say "in Sarajevo at least," because I'm very aware that the JNA was operating in Bosanska Krajina fighting the Croatians. That's why the "at least" is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you also aware that the JNA was actively engaged in distributing arms to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you also are -- must be aware that on March 2nd, when the crisis occurred, that was shown in the BBC film - and it looked like a putsch was about to take place - Izetbegovic escaped the worst possible situation then because the General -- General -- I won't -- because the JNA general supported Izetbegovic. And this is March 2nd. And furthermore, he had -- Izetbegovic had negotiations with the JNA on -- in -- later, in which JNA -- which is in the book here, in Skopje, in Macedonia, where they tried to reach some kind of continuation of political talks. All of this referred to one segment of the JNA - I forget the general's name, excuse me - in Sarajevo, who was indeed trying to mediate between the various sides in the conflict in the city. That is at least on the basis of my information. If I'm wrong, I hope you will correct me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that -- as you saw, we saw rightly, General Kukanjac was --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kukanjac. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- negotiating. But the JNA, by and large, was actively acting as a Serb army, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- it's important to know that the JNA itself was divided. Kukanjac was taking one position. The -- the forces -- the 5th Krajina Brigade in -- this is the kind of a thing that has to be explored. One can't -- one has to be careful of one's generalisations about these matters.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: My research suggests that persons within the JNA were not all in agreement with one another what to do. I may -- further research may prove me wrong, but for the moment that's where I stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But that's exactly the point, isn't it, Professor Shoup, that you haven't engaged in further research before you make these statements by, for example -- for example, examining the documents from the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no problem here. We know what the 1st Krajina Corps was doing. We know it was fighting in Croatia. When I was asked yesterday about what the position was of these soldiers and their morale, it seemed to me that it was quite possible that they were worried -- or preparing themselves to fight the other side when they were -- there's just no debate about what the 1st Krajina Corps -- I don't see why we have to consider more documents. Let's say -- but there is the fact that in -- in -- in Skopje on May 26th there was a tremendous effort made by the JNA to try and mediate the -- the - or was it April 26th, excuse me - the conflict. This is also a fact. You could ask me, Why don't I -- why didn't I look at the documents on that meeting in Skopje as well? I would love to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would like you just to have a look at one document, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Sure.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just have to slow down. I'm sorry. My apologies to the translators. I'll try to do better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we'll put the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I've noticed Mr. Ackerman standing up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I anticipated what it was. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to go, please -- this is a full report on the assessment of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume this is after the reorginisation of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, this is not. If you look at the date, it's March 1992.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say in your report -- while we're dealing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Usher, we need to see this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You state in your report that the VRS was formed on the 20th of May. May I suggest to you that you're wrong on that; it was on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you read the assembly meeting for the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Please have a look, would you. This is a full report, JNA, pre-VRS, to page 5.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you can see, it's not just the Krajina Corps, because it's personnel strength of the 9th, the 10th, the 5th, the 17th, and the 4th.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then it says, under F: "The JNA has distributed 51.900 weapons (75%) and the SDS, 17.298 weapons."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this deals, the next paragraph, you may think deals with the army staying on the sidelines in Sarajevo. "To date, 300 automatic rifles have been distributed to retired military officers in Sarajevo (those who can be trusted)."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In the next three or four days, another 100 person wills be armed. These person wills defend, protect housing estates, building entrances," and so on.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you think if you had read that before you wrote that in your report, you might not have written that sentence, "The JNA, at least in Sarajevo, remained on the sidelines."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would not have changed that. I would have changed it to General Kukanjac perhaps to avoid this discussion that we're having now. After all, we're perfectly aware that the elements of the army at least set up artillery emplacements around Sarajevo before the war began. Which to me is even more, if you will, indicative that there were elements in the JNA getting ready to fight than what you've said here. In any case, I don't see that this is -- condemns the -- condemns the army in any way. They seem to be saying, "We'll give these arms to people to protect themselves." I might find some other motives for that. I just don't see any significance really in giving out 100 persons some -- some means of defending themselves. I really think that you have a much better case if you talk about the way they were placing heavy artillery around the area of Sarajevo, which they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Professor, the only point that I'm trying to point out to you -- I'm trying to make is that your sentence in the report that the JNA remained on the sidelines, from the documentary evidence that you've never seen is clearly not an accurate one. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- my apologies that I didn't mislead you clearly when you read the report. But the fact is that General Kukanjac was taking a different position and playing a role of great importance at that critical juncture in trying to keep the lid on the conflict in Sarajevo. And yes, we might have -- I should have perhaps put his name in there instead of saying loosely "the JNA." I thought that -- that if he was -- if it was General Kukanjac, he was the JNA in Sarajevo. I guess, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you go, please, in your report now to page 24.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] One moment, because Judge Taya is asking me about the ethnicity of General Kukanjac. Was he a Serb -- of Serb --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name is not a Serbian name. But I wouldn't want to conclude just from that that he was a non-Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, could you go, please, to the bottom. The very last sentence.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We now know..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "We now know that in the period between March and September 1991 Milosevic had decided that all Serb majority areas, both in Bosnia and Croatia, should become Serbia proper."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How do we know that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). Mind you, that is a little bit off the cuff. But most of what we know about the changes that Milosevic made in his policies towards the Croatian war come from that source. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the answer is?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's -- I believe, without checking the book --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, why didn't you -- when you say, "We now know," why didn't you give the footnote for that assertion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess I don't understand. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). If -- I said, "We now know," meaning that somehow I'd got the information recently. No, I don't mean that. I'm looking at it from a ten-year perspective, I guess. (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't think he's answered your question, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think he has either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to know why, when you made an assertion isn't it not the most standard form of writing a book, an article, if you make an assertion such as "we now know" to give in a footnote from what "we now know." In

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, in other words you think there should be a footnote there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you, Professor Shoup, whether you don't think there should be a footnote there.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sure. I thought this was something that was in all in the literature and there are so many books on this subject. I thought this was common knowledge. But yes, for the Court it should have been footnoted. Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to page 25.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that's where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 25. The end of paragraph 3: "The irony is that if both parties had agreed to undertake population transfers as a means of avoiding a war between them, the International Community might not have become involved even if the local Croat and Muslim populations resisted displacement."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to know what you mean by that particular sentence.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am suggesting to the Court, as someone looking at the -- the history of this region -- that if the Serbs and the Croatians had agreed to a solution, including the partitioning of Bosnia in some fashion, and accomplished this as a fait accompli in a situation in which the International Community did not want to become involved in the Balkans, it's -- it's possible to speculate here - because speculation is in order - it reveals the complexities to have situation - it's possible that they could have gotten away with it. You can dispute this, but I think it sheds light on the fact that, one, there was a lack of agreement between Serbia and Croatia, which was critical to the outbreak of war in Bosnia; and secondly, that the International Community was desperate to find things -- sort themselves out peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what I want to know is this: By saying, "Even if the local Croat and Muslim populations resisted displacement --"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause and wait for the question, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you intending to say there that it would have been all right forcibly to move out the Muslim and Croats from where they had lived, as we've been told over and over again for centuries?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the irony in that sentence is -- and what I'm trying to say is that ethnic cleansing, which we attacked so vociferously and so correctly, because I consider this a crime, that what would have amounted to ethnic cleansing, population displacements done discreetly by discrimination against persons, making it unpleasant for them to stay in a place, might not have been so objectionable to the International Community if it had avoided the -- if it had avoided the outbreak of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may dispute, this but this is my cynical view of the actions of the great powers vis-a-vis this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you are saying in your view it would have been all right if population displacements done discreetly by discrimination against persons making it unpleasant or them to stay in a place might not have been so objectionable?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that is precisely what I did not say. I said a moment ago that the irony of the situation is that it would have been acceptable to the powers of Europe and the United States. I didn't say it was acceptable to me. I said this is what the history of this region is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm asking you. You are not, are you, saying that it was accept -- that it would have been acceptable for Muslims and Croats to have been forced to move out either, as you put it, by force or by discrimination? You're not saying that's acceptable?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how can you misunderstand the paper? I go into the fact that because Milosevic and Tudjman could only come up with a scheme for partition that involved population displacements it would -- it was unacceptable. I said that if they could have come up with a scheme which would have allowed Bosnia to remain in a "krnja" Yugoslavia, a rump Yugoslavia, without displacements, thereby preserving the multicultural heritage of Bosnia, that to me would have been the best solution. And I make it clear in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: See, the reason I ask you this - and I'm going to jump ahead for one moment - is what you say later on in this report, when you're dealing with ethnic cleansing. And I'll just find it for one moment. Page 37, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, third paragraph: "The phenomenon of ethnic cleansing --"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... in Bosnia was indeed a challenge to the International Community and those -- to those who had held up Bosnia as a model of ethnic toleration." This is the sentence that I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Yet ethnic cleansing was also a rational response within limits for combatants aiming to claim areas of mixed population or wishing to consolidate territory won in battle." Is that your view, Professor Shoup?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's my view. I wrote it. I say that it was a rational response, within limits, for combatants aiming to claim areas of mixed population, if they did claim areas of mixed population - which is hardly surprising that that's the case - "Or wishing to consolidate territory won in battle." I don't see anything remarkable about that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what are the limits that you would set?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The limits with which we're very familiar; that is, the -- mind you, I'm saying that it's no longer a rational response. I'm not saying it's a good or bad response. It's not a rational response. If population displacements or removing people from certain areas and putting them in safe places, like we did in World War II with the Japanese, it's not a rational response if it's done with brutality. If it's -- if it's not -- I don't like the response to begin with. I should slow down. I don't like the whole idea. But I'm talking about the difference between taking civilian populations, moving them about. It's been done in wartime time and time again, on the one hand, and the non-rational response, which is to plunder, which is to burn, which is to kill, these are not -- it's not a question of whether these non-rational responses are acceptable. The whole thing smells badly. But there is a very important distinction for the Court, certainly, between actions taken in time of war, vis-a-vis certain populations, and brutally or otherwise. And that's what this refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not -- I'd forgotten that Mr. Ackerman asked if we could rise early. And so I won't be able to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I mean, what -- how much longer do you think you need, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to need at least another couple of hours. I really -- I'd forgotten about one of the videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the reason why -- why I'm -- I've interrupted you is precisely because of this: We have agreed that we'd stop at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would think the interpreters would like a short break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I -- it's not my intention to deprive the interpreters or anyone else, for that matter, from a short break. How much would that leave us?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we would say 15 minutes or 10 minutes, perhaps would be sufficient, if we're going to stop at 1.15 in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like -- I can't see behind the dark glass panes. It's okay. So shall we have a ten-minute break now and then conclude at quarter past 1.00. And then the understanding is that Ms. Korner will continue with the witness on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think there were matters that both you and Ms. Korner wanted to raise before we broke. I'm wondering if you want to release the witness now or if we do ten minutes with the witness and then ten minutes -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I only needed less than five minutes, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I just want to inform Your Honour of one problem. So I won't take more than five minutes all told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's just scheduling of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a ten-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back on Monday to this question of ethnic cleansing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back on Monday to this question of ethnic cleansing. But I want to continue on the subject of the army, please. Page 29 of your report.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where you state in the top paragraph: "Placing all the blame on the VRS for the ethnic cleansing in the late spring and summer of 1992," and pausing there for a moment, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You do not know the detail, do you, of the actions undertaken by the VRS in Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, any one of those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know more now than I did when I read the report, having access to some of the testimony here. I don't think this -- I didn't think that I was saying anything that I could not say when I wrote this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what do you mean read --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a problem with something I've said?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, pause for a moment. Pause please, Professor Shoup. "I know more now than I did when I read the report"? What report? Do you mean when you wrote the report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wrote the report. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This report. What have you read since you wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have been reading, as you know, these materials that just -- you're asking me at what particular point in time I was looking at something on Prijedor or -- some of that came in my reviewing of the material that I had already read for the purposes of this report, because it's tremendous. As you know, the CIA is two huge volumes and so forth. And then in my hotel room, continuing to look at these reports for other things that might be interesting or noticing something -- something that might have been perhaps in Mr. Ackerman's office. I have come to see in more detail to these -- these events. For example, there is in that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop for a moment, please, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said: "I know more now than I did when I read the report, having access to some of the testimony here." What testimony have you read since you wrote that sentence on page 29 in your report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's see. You see, I -- I will have to take a step back. I'm not sure. I think there was -- one place I know that was very interest, was the CIA "Balkan Battlegrounds" annex which Mr. Ackerman brought to my attention, which gave a detailed description of one such incident in one particular village. I thought it was very interesting. I didn't -- hadn't used that or noticed it in -- in my report when I first looked at that volume. So there were just -- it seems to me that I was convinced that there was ethnic cleansing. My interest in writing the report at that time was not so much what happened in Prijedor or in Sanski Most. I was interested in that, of course, but when, because for this report it's important to know whether it took place in April, May, or June. And as I look at this and say -- I thought late spring and summer, May -- this would refer to May/June. I now see that some of this ethnic cleansing and specific incidents began a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Shoup, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to make your life more difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But -- no, no, it's not slowing down. It's answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you haven't answered the question. The question put to you was a very simple one: What testimony have you read since you wrote this sentence on page 29 in your report? And that's what Ms. Korner wants to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, let me think a minute. Since I've been looking at so many documents in this past week, which of those are new to me. It would take a moment for me to -- let's see. It seems to me -- yes, I can say this for a certain -- for a certainty: The Brown material and the -- the Treanor material I read here. I had -- they were not sent to me at the time I was reading the report. Now, Mr. Ackerman would know best what he sent me, but that's my recollection. That's -- that's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you've -- I'm sorry. Let's get this quite clear. You have read since you arrived here Dr. Treanor's evidence or his report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. It's the -- it's the testimony, not the report. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you've read Mr. Brown's --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
