utterances.text: Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I wish that Defence counsel would -- would perhaps clarify this. He might remember better. I don't think he sent that material to me in Charlottesville. I think I read it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, anyhow, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The VRS as formed on the 20th of May." I suggest to you you're wrong in that. It was officially formed at the end of the 12th of May assembly session. Was that a document shown to you by Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the VRS was formed on May 20th?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The VRS formally came into being on the 12th of May, I suggest to you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I'm asking you whether Mr. Ackerman showed you the minutes of the 12th of May assembly.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. "After the last of the non-Bosnian Serbs had left the ranks of the JNA." How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see. "After the last of the non-Bosnian Serbs had left the ranks of the JNA." All right. That was based on the assumption that the reorginisation of the JNA in Bosnia, as we know, to become an all-Serb organisation had begun as early as December of 1991. And I now see from some of the -- maybe it's the Treanor or Brown testimony -- that there was actually a dispute going on between the ARK, on the one hand, and the -- I guess it was the VRS about certain Muslims that were still left in the -- in the army. So I would have to -- to say that there were still a scattering of these people in the army. The basis of that was my assumption that they had left by that time, but not the basis of a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, I'm sorry, Professor Shoup, surely it is completely wrong in academic circles to put down an -- as an -- first of all, an assumption by you and then as a statement of fact.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should have been based on -- on empirical evidence of what happened at that time. This was careless, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you aware from your reading of testimony that there were Muslim and Croat officers serving in the VRS well after its formation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am now, yes. I wasn't aware at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "An order by Karadzic placing all paramilitary and TO forces under the command of the VRS was not issued until June and was not completely enforced for three to four weeks after, according to Karadzic himself."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Footnote 71: "On the formation of the VRS, see CIA ""Balkan Battlegrounds" Volume II."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The implementation of the June order based on information supplied the author." What information?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. By someone who had an interview with Karadzic on this particular matter, a very reliable source. I don't know if I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who's that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obrad Kesic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obrad Kesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why didn't you footnote that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This -- this is important, isn't it? You agree this is an important assertion.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was -- my mind was concentrated on the bigger issues. Yes, we could have certainly proved that, put Obrad Kesic's name on. Although I admit I was a little reluctant to do that unless it was necessary, but sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Part of the thesis of this report is, isn't it, is that there were "out of control" paramilitaries who were responsible for the offences?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take a step back for a moment and clarify what I'm doing. I started out trying to summarise the findings of our book about the historical background of Bosnia. I then thought that the Court probably did not have access to the very latest information on the Bosnian war and I was going to try to add that to my report, which is what I did here by citing Bosnian -- the CIA "Balkan Battlegrounds." I myself was confused by what I found. I found that these very valuable sources don't often speak with one voice. I thought this was important and useful to the Court to be able to see that in -- in the report, and that's what this is all about. It's not my belief, necessarily, that we know the answer to this question. There is counter-evidence that there were paramilitaries of at least one side or another who were acting out of control. But it's a warning. It's a warning that the latest materials from the CIA and other sources seemed to be contradictory about this phenomena, not my judgement. I'm not -- I'm only repeating what these people have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's right. You're relying - and we go back to where we started sometime earlier today - you're relying on the CIA book of which you have no knowledge and have not checked the sources yourself. When I say "no knowledge," of the information that's contained in this report.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't understand. Of course I've looked at the report. But I've looked -- that is, I've looked at the CIA volume, if that's what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, no, I'm not. You yourself --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- have had no opportunity to check the sources that the CIA used --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see what you mean. Of course. Of course not. And that's why I freely quote what are actually contradictory positions taken by the CIA to raise a red flag and hope that somebody will see that red flag and delve into this matter further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally on this page - and it's probably the last topic we can deal with today - "Furthermore" - this is one paragraph down - "the literature we have consulted --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- "seems unsure about accountability of military commanders for units which may have been normally operating under their command." What literature?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: What follows, the Shrader book. And when I say "the literature we have consulted," you know what it is. It's the CIA, it's the Dutch report. And here - I didn't mention this earlier - but this is very interesting Charles Shrader book, "The Muslim-Croat Civil War in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so, you're talking about, because you don't specify here, the CIA report, this book by Charles Shrader.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's evident if you look at what I've cited in the course of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did it ever occur to you to see if there were instructions that were current at the time about what commanders should do?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been delighted to see such instructions. Again, I was faced with the -- with a dilemma, you know, of what would be most useful to the Court. I decided the most useful thing was not to go into areas which you knew better than I did. You've seen all that -- those documents. But, rather, to bring you up to date on what the most authoritative and most recent and exhaustive studies are saying. They presumably have looked at the same material you have; I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But why, rather than a source which is filtered in some form or another, why not go to the original document? It -- just a moment -- which would show you clearly the instructions that were issued to military commanders?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could clone myself, I would be delighted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But isn't it -- is it fair. Just a moment, Mr. Ackerman. Is it fair to say that your preference at all times is to rely on secondary studies rather than original material?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you before that sometimes secondary sources are more reliable than primary sources if the secondary source is someone who has spent a great deal of time working over material which you might work over and not understand. I don't understand military terminology. I assume the CIA does. I would put much more faith in their descriptions than my own of -- if it was a primary source dealing with battalion X, Y, and Z. Secondary sources in this war are extremely important. You have to -- and maybe even more reliable on occasion than primary sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are -- we are repeating here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there you are. That's what I was being -- being -- we get back to this subject. I'm not sure why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Korner. Professor Shoup, it has been a long day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even though we are finishing earlier. But you deserve a rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will see you again on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we hope to finish on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. May I just perhaps ask Your Honours to remind Mr. Shoup that he's in the middle of giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shoup -- sorry, Professor Shoup, you are in the middle of giving evidence, so you should refrain from talking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. It's very important. And I appreciate it. And I should like to ask the -- my helper here just a question. Can I pose a question to the Judge without violating protocol?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found that the document that I was asked to look at earlier by the JNA was extremely interesting, and I'm wondering if the Court can provide me again the number and how I can access it myself. I will address that to you and not to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is 1275 or something like that. I don't remember the number by heart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anyway, this is just minor matter but I would love to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it a problem with you, Ms. Korner if we photocopy it for him?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just have a chance to think about that over the weekend?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only reason I hesitate is because it comes from the 1st Krajina Corps collection, and I'm not sure the status of it. Some of the collections are on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I just want a chance to check.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps it's -- some way that somebody can tell me how to access it. Because there's an electronic jungle out there and it's awfully hard to know how to do it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Professor Shoup. You will be escorted to your hotel and we'll see you again Monday. Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I thank the Prosecution for providing me with the full text in English. I have this pasted on my wall, by the way, in my study because I think it's such a remarkable document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we need -- it's a case of discussing a little bit our scheduling for this coming week. Monday will be taken by -- by this witness, and we hope to finish. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will. I will finish on Monday. There's no question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's Monday. Now, we have your witness in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, that's the problem. Can I go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we really did agree that we would finish at 1.15. And we can deal with this liter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry that this hurts Ms. Korner's case but it's in evidence. And she's had the whole case to deal with it and now to say it's a temporary exhibit and shouldn't be included in the case is just preposterous. It was put in evidence when Dr. Donia was testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I have never considered it to be tendered as temporarily. I mean, that was not my impression. And correct me if I'm wrong and please come back to us first thing Monday morning. But it was not my impression that it was being tendered by -- by the Defence provisionally or subject to our deciding --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't dealing with -- I don't know. I'll have to check the transcript myself. Because Mr. Cayley dealt with Dr. Donia's evidence, as you may recall. And Your Honour, I agree -- Mr. Ackerman has an point. But I think this matter needs to be dealt with in a little more depth as a matter of legal argument as to what, if any, is the relevance of this book to the issues that Your Honours have to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the other publication s that Mr. Ackerman wishes to enter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll just close with the phrase: You're professional Judge, you can to sort it out. That has -- this record to be just clobbered up with all kinds of material that the Prosecutor has given you that I think you shouldn't be looking at either, but that's your position and I think you have to be consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's good to know that a lawyer of such calibre as you, Mr. Ackerman, holds us in such high esteem. Thank you. And have a nice --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
